title: Franklin's chart
hookLine: Benjamin Franklin tracked thirteen virtues, one a week, with a dot for every slip (Autobiography)

lines: A BLACK DOT FOR EVERY SLIP.
cards: Before habit apps, before streaks and badges, a young printer in Philadelphia made himself a little book. He ruled each page in red ink: columns for the days of the week, rows for thirteen virtues.
Every evening he went down the rows and put a small black dot wherever he'd slipped. That printer was Benjamin Franklin, years before most people knew his name.
He tells the story in his Autobiography, and he's funny about it, because it did not go the way he planned.

teach.b: Franklin says he set out, boldly, to arrive at moral perfection. He listed thirteen virtues, each with a short rule. Temperance: don't eat or drink to excess.
Tranquility. Chastity. And humility, which he added later, after a friend told him, kindly, that he was proud.
His clever move: he didn't try all thirteen at once.
He gave each virtue one week of close attention, while just marking the others, so he got through the list in thirteen weeks, four times a year. How did it go?

teach.h: FULLER OF FAULTS THAN I IMAGINED.
teach.b: He was surprised to find himself, in his own words, so much fuller of faults than I had imagined. The dots piled up.
Order, keeping his papers and hours in their places, cost him so much effort that he was almost ready to give up on it.
He compares himself to a man who wanted his whole axe polished bright, got tired of turning the grinding wheel, and decided he liked a speckled axe best. And yet the ending is gentle.

He never reached perfection, he says, but the attempt made him a better and happier man than he would otherwise have been. The chart turns this week's evening review into something you can see, and adds one idea: focus.
Not every fault, every night. One virtue, for one week, noticed closely. Small enough to actually do.

how: Franklin's method from his Autobiography is still copied by some people who keep habit trackers: a short list of virtues, one given close attention each week, with a mark each evening for every slip.

practice: Let a few of Franklin's virtues pass through your mind, patience, order, silence, sincerity, humility, or one of your own, and pick the one that would make the biggest small difference this week.
Picture one moment tomorrow where it would matter, then let the choice rest. No chart required, though a scrap of paper with seven boxes wouldn't hurt.
